grades.reason: Discusses xv6 paging limitations, super pages, ASIDs and allocators. It never explains why a sparse virtual address space uses little physical memory.

grades.quote: If a PTE in a first or second level page directory page isn’t valid, then the required directory page hasn’t yet been allocated; if the alloc argument is set, walk allocates a new page-table page and puts its physical address in the PTE.
grades.reason: Describes the RISC-V multi-level page table walk. Directory pages are allocated only when needed, and invalid PTEs mean nothing is allocated, so unused regions of the address space cost no physical memory. It never states the sparse-address-space point explicitly.

grades.quote: to keep its size manageable, the table does not independently list a physical address for each virtual address.
grades.reason: Explains that virtual memory uses a table mapping pages to page frames, not a rule applied to every address. This is general background for the answer, but it does not address sparseness or unmapped regions.

grades.quote: Moreover, the mappings between virtual and physical addresses need not be established in advance. By marking pages as illegal to access, and then making them available when an interrupt indicates that they are first accessed, the operating system can provide mappings on a demand-driven basis.
grades.reason: Says mappings need not be set up in advance. Pages can be marked illegal and mapped on demand when first accessed, so virtual addresses with no mapping use no physical memory. This is a useful part of the answer, but it does not mention page-table structure or the word sparse.
